Llantarnam
hlan-TAR-nam
n. (a Cistercian abbey in Monmouthshire, Wales, founded 1179; custodian of the pilgrimage shrine and image of Penrhys)
Welsh llan, a church enclosure, with the local name Tarnam; the house was also called Dewma or Caerleon, from its first site.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Llantarnam was founded in 1179 by Hywel ab Iorwerth, lord of Caerleon, as a daughter of Strata Florida. Its chief business in the later Middle Ages was not farming but a shrine: the abbey owned and served the image of Our Lady of Penrhys on the ridge between the Rhondda valleys, the most frequented pilgrimage in south Wales, with a holy well below it and a steady income from offerings. In 1538 the image was taken to London and burnt at Chelsea on Cromwell's orders. The second commandment is not ambiguous about what was burnt: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4). Isaiah's satire is sharper, because he follows the workman through the process until the leftover wood becomes the god, and then “he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god” (Isa 44:17). The prophet's verdict on the worshipper is not contempt but pity: “a deceived heart hath turned him aside, that he cannot deliver his soul” (Isa 44:20).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines image as a representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; and idol as an image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship.

expand to see more

IMAGE, n. A representation or similitude of any person or thing, formed of a material substance; as an image wrought out of stone, wood or wax.

IDOL, n. An image, form or representation, usually of a man or other animal, consecrated as an object of worship; a pagan deity.

SHRINE, n. A case, box or repository in which sacred things are deposited; as the shrine of a saint.

PILGRIMAGE, n. A long journey, particularly a journey to some place deemed sacred and venerable, in order to pay devotion to the relics of some deceased saint.

VOTIVE, a. Given by vow; devoted; as a votive offering.

Key Scripture

Exo 20:4 — "Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the water under the earth:"

Exo 20:5 — "Thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me;"

Isa 44:17 — "And the residue thereof he maketh a god, even his graven image: he falleth down unto it, and worshippeth it, and prayeth unto it, and saith, Deliver me; for thou art my god."

Isa 44:20 — "He feedeth on ashes: a deceived heart hath turned him aside, that he cannot deliver his soul, nor say, Is there not a lie in my right hand?"

Modern Corruption

A Welsh abbey whose real income was a hilltop image, and the commandment that burnt it.

expand to see more

The corruption is the devotional economy — a house of prayer sustained by offerings made to a carved figure. The defence always offered is that the honour passes through the image to the person represented; Isaiah does not accept the distinction, and neither does the commandment, which forbids the making and the bowing in the same breath and attaches to it the words “for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God” (Exo 20:5). The economic fact is the giveaway: the offerings went to the shrine that had the image, not to the one that did not.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the second commandment protects the worshipper, not God's dignity alone. Isaiah ends his satire with a man who cannot ask the one question that would free him: “Is there not a lie in my right hand?” (Isa 44:20). The modern images are not carved, but the structure is identical wherever devotion attaches to a thing that can be owned, housed and charged for.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Welsh llan, a church enclosure; Hebrew pesel (H6459), a graven image; Hebrew temunah (H8544), a likeness; Hebrew qanna (H7067), jealous; Hebrew sheqer (H8267), a lie.

expand to see more

Welsh llan — a consecrated enclosure, a church site.

Hebrew pesel (H6459) — a carved or graven image; “any graven image” (Exo 20:4).

Hebrew temunah (H8544) — a likeness, a form; “or any likeness of any thing that is in heaven above” (Exo 20:4).

Hebrew qanna (H7067) — jealous; “for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God” (Exo 20:5).

Hebrew sheqer (H8267) — falsehood, a lie; “Is there not a lie in my right hand?” (Isa 44:20).

Usage

"“Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exo 20:4) — the law the shrine broke."

"“Deliver me; for thou art my god” (Isa 44:17) — said on a Welsh ridge for three centuries."

"“He feedeth on ashes” (Isa 44:20) — the prophet's diagnosis, not his insult."
